name: Hyoid / neck posture meta

lead: The hyoid meta is the belief that a low hyoid bone, forward neck posture and submental fat blunt the angle between chin and neck. People work on it for a sharper under-chin line and a cleaner jawline in profile.

The hyoid is a horseshoe-shaped bone in the front of the neck, held by muscles and ligaments. Medical literature on its position concerns breathing and swallowing, and a lower hyoid is associated with obstructive sleep apnea. No study has tested whether exercises move the hyoid or change neck contour.

paras: Users combine chin tucks, neck and posture exercises and tongue posture with fat loss to reduce under-chin fullness, and check results in profile photos. Some also discuss submental injections or liposuction.
No harms are documented for the exercises themselves in the sources reviewed. Related procedures such as submental injections or liposuction are medical interventions with their own risks.

angle.text: The goal is a sharper chin-to-neck angle and cleaner profile through neck posture work, chin tucks and reducing under-chin fat. Hyoid research concerns airway anatomy, so the link to appearance comes from forum theory.

lead: The hyoid or neck posture meta is a set of ideas in looksmaxxing communities holding that the position of the hyoid bone, together with neck posture and the fat under the chin, determines how sharp the jawline and neck look in profile. Users describe a "low" or "bad" hyoid as flattening the angle between chin and neck, and a higher, tighter neck line as the goal. People pursue it through chin tucks and neck exercises, posture work, body-fat reduction, and, in some threads, cosmetic procedures aimed at the submental area [1].

The hyoid is a horseshoe-shaped bone in the front of the neck, between the chin and the thyroid cartilage, held in place by muscles and ligaments rather than by joints with other bones [2]. Medical literature on its position concerns breathing and swallowing rather than appearance: a lower hyoid is associated with obstructive sleep apnea [2][3][4]. No published study has tested whether exercises or posture change the visible neck contour by moving the hyoid in healthy people.

The topic overlaps with the broader idea of the cervicomental angle (the chin-to-neck angle), with submental fat, and with jaw and chin projection. Encyclopedia sources note that a double-chin look can come from excess fat or from a chin and jaw that sit far back relative to the neck, so forum users often discuss several variables together [5][6].

The idea sits next to other jawline and profile practices in looksmaxxing: mewing and tongue posture, body-fat reduction, chin and jaw surgery, and submental fat treatments. Plastic surgeons, orthodontists and sleep researchers each describe parts of the same anatomy in their own vocabulary, which is why the forum term 'hyoid' often stands in for a mix of bone position, muscle tone, fat and jaw projection [6][4][7].

paras: People who discuss the hyoid meta want a sharper side profile: a visible, well-defined angle between the underside of the chin and the neck, and a jawline that reads clearly from the side. Practices discussed under this heading include chin tucks and neck curls, posture work, general fat loss, and, for some, submental fat treatments or surgery [1][8].

Believers treat the neck as part of the facial frame: in one widely read thread, the argument is that a strong eye area, maxilla and nose are offset if the neck forms a steep slope under the chin [9]. In that framing, improving neck contour is a way to make the rest of the face read better in photographs and in person.

The hyoid sits in the midline of the neck, between the base of the mandible and the third cervical vertebra at rest, and is described as loosely tied to the skeleton through muscles and ligaments [2]. Muscles of the tongue, floor of the mouth, larynx and pharynx attach to it, including the geniohyoid, mylohyoid, sternohyoid and thyrohyoid [2]. It supports breathing, swallowing and speech and helps keep the upper airway open during sleep [2].

The bone ossifies gradually: the horns begin to ossify late in fetal development, and until middle age the junction between the body and the greater horns is fibrous before it usually becomes bony [2]. The hyoid develops from the second and third pharyngeal arches [2].

Reference sources on the hyoid do not discuss how it shapes the external neck or jawline [2]. In looksmaxxing discussion, the visible neck contour is attributed both to bone position and to soft tissue such as submental fat, which some forum users distinguish explicitly from "hyoid" [1][8]. Wikipedia's article on the double chin attributes the look in people of normal weight to a jaw that does not project far enough, and in some overweight people to a fold of fat under the chin [6].

Neck and chin-neck angle appear in plastic-surgery vocabulary long before looksmaxxing: surgical texts discuss the cervicomental angle when assessing neck contour, and a 1978 study is cited for the link between deep platysma support and a more defined angle [7]. The term 'hyoid' entered forum talk as a shorthand for the underlying bony and muscular position.

Wikipedia traces looksmaxxing to 2010s forums on which appearance rating scales and bone-structure vocabulary developed, with a spread to TikTok in the early 2020s [10]. Within that vocabulary, jaw-related practices cluster under 'softmaxxing' and 'hardmaxxing'. Mewing grew from the orthotropics of the British orthodontist John Mew (1928-2025), who proposed the 'Tropic Premise' in 1958 and argued that tongue posture shapes jaw growth; his son Mike Mew popularised the do-it-yourself version on social media [11].

Threads asking whether a low hyoid can be 'fixed' appear on looksmax.org through the 2020s, with titles such as one that asks if a hyoid problem is fixable and a 2022 thread titled 'Hyoid bone is law' [1][9].

Proponents state that hyoid height, neck length and neck posture set the visible chin-neck angle, that a lower or more prominent hyoid blunts the profile, and that exercise, tongue posture or reduced submental fat can improve the line. Some posters separate the 'hyoid' from submental fat and point to cases in which a lean person still has a soft neck line [1][8].

Others in the same threads reply with doubt, noting that neck appearance depends on jaw and chin projection and on soft tissue, and giving anecdotes of acquaintances with strong forward growth and little visible neck bulk [1][9].

In general terms, people discuss chin tuck and neck curl exercises, posture awareness (reducing forward head posture), lowering body fat, and tongue posture. Forward head posture is a common modern posture pattern associated with prolonged use of screens, and sources on it recommend strengthening the deep neck flexors and mid-back muscles and stretching the muscles that pull the neck forward [12].
Submental fat treatments are also discussed. This article does not reproduce procedural details; they are medical or cosmetic procedures performed by clinicians.
No studies found on hyoid position and facial or neck appearance in the general population. Related clinical research is on the airway and swallowing.

A meta-analysis of cephalometric studies found that adults with obstructive sleep apnea had a hyoid positioned lower and further from reference landmarks than people without the condition; weighted mean differences included roughly 5 to 7 mm on several distance measures, alongside a longer anterior lower face height and a narrower pharyngeal airway space [3].

A 2025 pilot trial of web-based orofacial myofunctional therapy in adults with sleep apnea reported improved hyoid position after 12 weeks; the study did not test mewing, according to a description of it [5]. Hyoid suspension is one of several skeletal procedures, alongside maxillomandibular advancement and genioglossus advancement, used in multilevel surgery for sleep apnea [13].

A systematic review of rehabilitation for stroke-related swallowing difficulty lists chin tuck against resistance exercise and electrical stimulation of hyoid muscles among the therapies used in 15 randomized trials; these studies concern swallowing function in patients, not neck appearance [14]. A 2025 meta-analysis of airway ultrasound (60 studies, 10,580 patients) examined measurements such as tongue thickness and skin-to-epiglottis distance in predicting difficult airways, again not appearance [15].

Cephalometric work on hyoid position is mostly cross-sectional. A 2025 study of 40 healthy adults found that nearly all hyoid parameters differed between neutral and forward head posture on lateral radiographs, which led the authors to say head posture should be considered when measuring hyoid position [4]. A 2025 retrospective cohort of 65 adults found hyoid position to be generally stable after surgically assisted palatal expansion, with changes under 2 mm that the authors judged clinically negligible [4].

A 2026 systematic review of 22 studies found that a lower hyoid position correlated with higher sleep apnea severity, with the distance from the hyoid to the mandibular plane the strongest predictor [4]. A 2025 case report described a patient who developed mild obstructive sleep apnea after about three weeks of daily chin tuck exercise, with symptoms resolving after stopping; as a single case it cannot establish causation [4].

On the soft-tissue side, a phase III randomised placebo-controlled trial of 363 people with moderate or severe submental fat found that clinician-rated responders reached 59.2 percent and 65.3 percent at two doses of injected deoxycholic acid, versus 23.0 percent with placebo [4]. The US FDA approved a deoxycholic acid injection for fat below the chin in 2015, and it is prescription-only [16]. A retrospective review of 180 neck lifts reported that 68 percent of patients had earlier non-surgical neck treatments and that fibrosis and altered tissue planes were common at later surgery [4].

On looksmax.org, the hyoid is a frequent topic, with thread titles asking how to raise, improve or fix it. Users describe a low hyoid as disrupting the side profile and ask whether chin tucks and neck curls change it, with some replies expressing doubt [1]. One widely read thread argues that even strong eye area, maxilla and nose are offset if the neck forms a steep slope under the chin [9]. Other users reply with anecdotes about acquaintances with strong forward growth and little visible neck bulk [9].

Submental fat reduction through surgery or injected fat-dissolving products is also discussed in these threads, with some users recommending liposuction by a surgeon over injections [8]. This article does not reproduce procedural details.

The term sits within the wider bonehacks category, which also includes tongue-posture practices such as mewing. Orthodontic organizations, as summarized in one encyclopedia, state that there is no credible evidence that tongue posture reshapes the face or jaw [5].
The overall tone of these threads mixes anxiety about a feature that users consider fixed with debate about whether anything can change it [1][9].

Cosmetic surgery sources describe a 'hyoid lift' as a surgical approach that removes the fat pad under the chin and shortens certain jaw muscles, usually for cosmetic reasons. Chin surgery (genioplasty) and orthognathic surgery that moves the jaws forward are described as options where the issue is a recessed chin or jaw [6].

Neck lift surgery may include platysmaplasty, which tightens or repositions the platysma muscle; reported risks include haematoma, numbness, temporary nerve weakness, contour irregularities and recurrent bands, and over-resection of fat can cause a 'cobra neck' deformity [7]. Injected deoxycholic acid acts by breaking down fat cells in the submental region [16], and a 2026 review notes that poor injection technique can cause skin necrosis and marginal mandibular nerve palsy [4].

Anatomy references and the airway literature treat hyoid position as a marker of upper-airway anatomy, and hyoid suspension is a surgical procedure used in sleep apnea [2][13]. Mainstream orthodontic organizations, as summarized in one encyclopedia, state that there is no credible evidence that tongue-posture practices such as mewing reshape the face or jaw [5].

lore.intro: The hyoid is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a presumed determinant of side-profile neck definition, often alongside submental fat and neck posture [1].
